A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WeightWatch research. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: Sections 4–6 and the appendices report original backdoor detection, unlearning, steering, and model-auditing experiments.

after.justification: Original experiments are retained, alongside retrained backdoor-model results, behavioral validation, and additional evaluations.

M1.justification: The SVD-based behavioral vectors, monitoring rules, and steering algorithm remain unchanged. The auditing workflow changes from embedding/HDBSCAN clustering and GPT-4o-mini summaries to per-direction GPT-5.1 annotations using ten transcripts from each extremal tail, followed by inspection and keyword search (v2 Appendix F.1; v3 Appendix E.1).

E1.justification: v3 adds LMSYS-Chat-1M false-positive evaluation, GSM8K and HellaSwag utility tests, AIME 2025 reasoning-style evaluation, and emoji-appropriate prompts. Training-data attribution expands to OLMo's DPO data; the separate ShareGPT analysis disappears while OLMo SFT analysis remains.

E2.justification: BEAT is newly compared against WeightWatch on the FFT backdoor checkpoints in v3 Table 6; v2's corresponding Table 7 reports only WeightWatch. The PPO comparator membership remains BEAT and activation-difference norm. BEAT's additional operating point does not constitute another baseline.

E3.justification: Reported FFT training changes from five to three epochs, batch size eight to four, and peak learning rate 2×10^-4 to 10^-5 (v2 Appendix D.2; v3 Appendix C.3). v3 explicitly reports dataset regeneration and retraining, and expands badnet trigger configurations. Added protocols include BEAT at 10% FPR, 1,000 LMSYS prompts, 30 AIME problems, 50 emoji prompts, and sampled SFT/DPO relevance classification.

E4.justification: v3 adds a calibration-size/FPR analysis (Figure 8), reasoning-style and emoji behavioral checks (Section 6.3), and an annotation information-loss case study (Appendix E.2). OLMo attribution is reworked into semantic relevance checks. The original weight-subtraction ablation and KL-divergence analysis are retained.

E5.justification: The reported FFT badnet aggregate expands from five checkpoints of one trained model to fifteen checkpoints of three trained models. This changes reported run aggregation; the models use different trigger strings, rather than documented repeated seeds. Neither version reports confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces FFT results: ctba completion flagging changes from 56.43% to 100%, and mtba from 72.59% to 93.33%, under revised training conditions. Table 3 revises BEAT's PPO results, including trojan3 at 2% FPR from 1.0% to 31.95%. New results cover annotation frequencies, behavioral validation, LMSYS, GSM8K, and HellaSwag. Original unlearning results and relocated language/direct-transcript counts remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation in Section 3 and Appendix A's false-positive argument and rank-one gradient-update derivation are unchanged. The added calibration curve supplies empirical evidence without revising the theory.

C1.justification: The central unsupervised monitoring and control claims remain. The introduction raises the backdoor detection range from 56–100% to 93–100%, while the abstract tightens FPR from below 1.2% to below 1% and highlights emoji usage. The new detection range conflicts with the retained 66.67% LoRA mtba result in Table 2.

C2.justification: v3 substantially revises auditing interpretations, emphasizing reasoning, emoji usage, and behavioral validation. Section 6.4 explains why training-topic prevalence need not produce proportional behavioral directions; Appendices E.2/E.4 discuss annotation compression and ambiguous keywords. Earlier ShareGPT/Qwen marketing speculation and the LoRA-over-FFT robustness conclusion are removed. The general limitations statement is merely relocated.

D1.justification: v3 adds explicit base-model mappings, four-GPU/DeepSpeed training details, and annotation, sampling, and generation instructions and prompts. Documentation remains inconsistent: Section 6.4/Table 14 name GPT-4o-mini for relevance classification, whereas Appendices E.1/G name GPT-4.1-mini. Its retrospective FFT dataset account also conflicts with v2's already-described Gemma generation pipeline.

R1.justification: v3 adds Buyl et al. on model ideology and Zheng et al. on LMSYS-Chat-1M, while removing the standalone ShareGPT and Ivison et al. Tulu 2 references. The dedicated Related Works discussion remains unchanged; discovery positioning now additionally emphasizes Qwen's emoji preference.

P1.justification: Section 6 is extensively rewritten and reorganized around automated interpretation, behavioral validation, and data attribution. Case-study curation moves into Section 4, language statistics move to the appendix, and limitations/impact statements move after references. The core methodological exposition remains largely intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds annotation, base-model, and data-relevance tables plus an FPR curve, redraws the BEAT ROC plot, and expands result tables with BEAT, LMSYS, GSM8K, and HellaSwag columns. Existing language and direct-transcript tables are relocated, while the old Tulu/ShareGPT comparison display is removed.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens v2's noisy auditing evidence with direction-level examples, behavioral checks, and clearer implementation details, while broadening baseline and utility evaluation. These gains are limited by the unsupported 93–100% headline despite a retained 66.67% result, and conflicting dataset/classifier documentation. Higher FFT scores follow changed training conditions and therefore do not establish an improved detection algorithm.
